title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
This incident shows an AI coding and agent tool being used as an operational component inside an active ransomware campaign. The attackers ran Cursor Agent, which itself invoked Claude Sonnet, to assist with hands-on exploitation across multiple target organizations during a period of roughly six weeks. This is a case of a general-purpose AI tool being used outside the conditions it was built for, deployed by threat actors rather than legitimate users, and integrated into a multi-stage attack chain that also included custom scanning scripts and ESXi-specific encryption routines.

The failure is not a model hallucination or a flawed deployment by a vendor, but an adversarial misuse of a publicly available tool. The point in the pipeline where a guardrail might have intervened is at the level of the AI system itself, which would have required the model to detect and refuse exploitation-oriented prompts. Whether such prompts were phrased in ways that evaded content policies, or whether the policies simply did not cover the specific requests made, is not established by the reporting.

What is not established is the full scope of damage to affected organizations, whether any of the ten named targets suffered data loss or paid ransoms, and whether the tool's developers were aware of or took action in response to this use pattern before the research was published.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that Aurora ransomware, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi environments and is abusing an AI tool called Cursor Agent to conduct exploitation attacks. Between April 8 and May 21, 2026, Aurora operators used Cursor Agent running Claude Sonnet to assist with hands-on exploitation across ten target organizations. The ransomware uses ChaCha20 encryption with RSA-4096 key wrapping and includes an ESXi mode that kills virtual machines, encrypts their files, and leaves ransom notes accessible via SSH banner.

The attackers also deployed custom tools including esxi_finder.py to scan networks for ESXi hypervisors and vCenter servers. A second cluster of Aurora activity was identified with medium confidence, affecting eight victim organizations across multiple countries including Israel, Germany, Austria, Spain, the United States, and Argentina. This second group used different tactics involving SQL Server exploitation, privilege escalation, and data exfiltration to self-hosted S3 storage. Gambit Security published indicators of compromise including IP addresses, domains, and file hashes to help organizations identify Aurora's infrastructure.
